<!-- Section 2: Theory -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-theory">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">01 · Signal Theory</div>
<h2>2.1 Mathematical Foundations of Discrete Fourier Analysis</h2>
<p>In mechanical condition monitoring, continuous sensor voltages $x(t)$ (from accelerometers or strain gauges) are sampled discretely at uniform sampling rate $f_s = 1/\Delta t$.</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="card-title">Continuous vs. Discrete Transforms</div>
<p>
The continuous Fourier transform maps a continuous signal $x(t)$ into continuous complex frequency spectra:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) e^{-i 2\pi f t} \, dt, \quad x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(f) e^{i 2\pi f t} \, df$$
</div>

<p>
For digital signal acquisition with $N$ discrete measurements sampled at interval $\Delta t$:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] \exp\left(-i \frac{2\pi k n}{N}\right), \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1$$
</div>

<div class="callout-note">
<div class="callout-title">Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Criterion & Aliasing</div>
<p>
The continuous signal frequency spectrum is unambiguously captured only up to the Nyquist folding frequency:
</p>
$$f_{\text{Nyq}} = \frac{f_s}{2} = \frac{1}{2\Delta t}$$
<p>
Any high-frequency content above $f_{\text{Nyq}}$ will fold back (alias) into the lower frequency spectrum, masquerading as spurious low-frequency vibrations! Always employ hardware analog anti-aliasing low-pass filters prior to ADC digitization.
</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 4: Pedagogical Misconception Callout -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-misconceptions">
<div class="callout-important">
<div class="callout-title">
<svg width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M10.29 3.86L1.82 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.71 3h16.94a2 2 0 0 0 1.71-3L13.71 3.86a2 2 0 0 0-3.42 0z"/><line x1="12" y1="9" x2="12" y2="13"/><line x1="12" y1="17" x2="12.01" y2="17"/></svg>
Common Misconception · Does Zero-Padding Improve Frequency Resolution?
</div>
<p style="margin: 0 0 8px 0;">
A widespread misconception among junior data analysts is that appending zeros to a sampled vibration vector improves the true physical frequency resolution of an FFT.
</p>
<p style="margin: 0;">
<strong>It does not.</strong> True physical frequency resolution $\Delta f$ is strictly determined by the total observation duration: $\Delta f = 1/T = 1/(N \Delta t)$. Appending zeros merely interpolates intermediate points along the continuous Fourier transform (sinc-curve interpolation) without adding a single bit of new information. To distinguish two tightly spaced mechanical modes (e.g., $100.0\text{ Hz}$ and $100.5\text{ Hz}$), you must record for a longer duration ($T \ge 2.0\text{ seconds}$).
</p>
</div>
</section>

<strong>Question:</strong> An engineer samples gearbox vibration at $f_s = 2000\text{ Hz}$ for $T = 0.5\text{ seconds}$. What is the physical frequency resolution $\Delta f$ and the maximum detectable frequency without aliasing?
</div>
<div class="quiz-options">

</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="true" data-explanation="Physical frequency bin spacing is Delta f = 1/T = 1/0.5 s = 2.0 Hz. The Nyquist frequency limit is fs / 2 = 2000 / 2 = 1000 Hz.">
B. $\Delta f = 2.0\text{ Hz}$, $f_{\max} = 1000\text{ Hz}$.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Delta f is reciprocal of total duration T, not 1/fs. 1/fs = 0.0005 s is the time sampling step!">

<!-- Section 6: Code -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-code">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">04 · Computational Implementation</div>
<h2>2.4 FFT Implementation in Python & MATLAB</h2>
<p>Perform windowed FFT analysis and plot single-sided amplitude spectra.</p>
</div>

<div class="code-box">
<div class="code-header">
<div class="code-tabs">
<button class="code-tab-btn active">Python (NumPy / SciPy)</button>
<button class="code-tab-btn">MATLAB</button>
</div>
<button class="btn-copy">Copy Code</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>import numpy as np
import scipy.signal as signal

# Sampling parameters
fs = 2000.0          # Sampling rate (Hz)
t = np.arange(0, 1.0, 1/fs)
N = len(t)

# Synthetic vibration signal with additive noise
x = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50.0 * t) + 1.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 180.0 * t)
x += 0.4 * np.random.normal(0, 1, N)

# Apply Hann window to suppress spectral leakage
window = np.hanning(N)
X_fft = np.fft.rfft(x * window)
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)
magnitude = np.abs(X_fft) * (2.0 / np.sum(window))

print(f"Sampling Rate: {fs} Hz | Resolution: {fs/N:.2f} Hz")
print(f"Dominant frequencies detected: {freqs[np.argsort(magnitude)[-3:]]} Hz")</code></pre>
<pre class="code-block" hidden><code>% MATLAB Implementation
fs = 2000;
t = 0:1/fs:1-1/fs;
N = length(t);
x = 2.0*sin(2*pi*50*t) + 1.2*sin(2*pi*180*t) + 0.4*randn(size(t));

w = hann(N)';
X = fft(x .* w);
P2 = abs(X / sum(w));
P1 = P2(1:N/2+1);
P1(2:end-1) = 2*P1(2:end-1);
f = fs*(0:(N/2))/N;

plot(f, P1, 'LineWidth', 1.8, 'Color', [0.7, 0.38, 0.16]);
xlabel('Frequency (Hz)'); ylabel('|P_1(f)|'); grid on;</code></pre>
</div>
